headline: Ferrari's first electric car fetches record $40m at Monterey auction
deck: The sale of the hand-built Luce chassis, designed by Jony Ive, marks the most expensive Ferrari ever auctioned and signals the brand’s pivot toward electrification.
body: Ferrari’s first electric car sold for $40 million at RM Sotheby’s Monterey Auction 2026, shattering records as the most expensive Ferrari ever auctioned. The hand-built Luce production chassis, designed by former Apple chief designer Jony Ive, commanded the staggering price in a sale that underscored the luxury brand’s aggressive push into electric vehicles. The final bid came amid fierce bidding war Thursday evening, with the car’s provenance as Ferrari’s inaugural EV driving demand to unprecedented levels. Analysts note the price reflects not just the car’s exclusivity but the broader appetite for high-end electrification among ultra-wealthy collectors. The result sends a clear signal: the future of supercar collecting is charging forward—literally.

The Luce’s production chassis—serial number 001—was the star lot in a weekend of high-profile sales at the Monterey Car Week, where vintage Ferraris and modern hypercars routinely fetch nine-figure prices. Unlike Ferrari’s existing hybrid models, the Luce is a full-electric reinterpretation of the brand’s classic 250-era styling, blending retro aesthetics with cutting-edge battery technology. Industry insiders describe the car as a rolling manifesto: proof that Ferrari can marry its storied craftsmanship with the demands of the 21st-century market. The $40 million result places it in rarefied company, alongside only a handful of cars—most of them pre-war Bugattis or one-off Mercedes—ever sold at auction.

Designed under the direction of Jony Ive during his tenure as Ferrari’s chief design advisor, the Luce represents a rare collaboration between the automotive and tech worlds. Ive’s involvement lent the project an almost Apple-like precision, with a minimalist interior, tactile carbon-fiber surfaces, and an interface that reimagines the driving experience for an electric era. While Ferrari has not confirmed production plans, the auction result suggests that demand for such a vehicle—even at a conceptually pure, one-off level—is off the charts. The price tag implies the car is as much a collectible as it is a drivable piece of art.

The auction, organized by RM Sotheby’s, took place under the floodlights of the Monterey Peninsula, where the world’s wealthiest car enthusiasts gather annually to trade trophies from the golden age of motoring. Bidding opened in the mid-twenties and escalated quickly, with phone and in-room bidders pushing the price past $30 million before a final, decisive jump sealed the deal. The winning bidder remains anonymous, but industry observers suggest they are either a legacy collector seeking a blue-chip asset or a tech titan placing a wager on Ferrari’s electric future.

Ferrari’s shift toward electrification has been both praised and scrutinized. Traditionalists argue that the brand risks diluting its racing DNA by moving away from internal combustion, while environmental advocates see the Luce as a necessary evolution for a company long criticized for its carbon footprint. The Monterey sale provides an early data point: electric Ferraris, when positioned as artisanal relics rather than mere transportation, can command prices that rival the most coveted combustion models in history. It’s a financial victory that may accelerate the brand’s broader electric strategy, including rumored production versions of the Luce due by 2030.

The Luce’s record sale comes at a pivotal moment for the luxury car market, where electric vehicles are increasingly treated as status symbols rather than environmental statements. Ferrari’s entry into the space with a car that looks and drives like a classic—only with silent, instant torque—has reframed the conversation around what an EV can represent. Collectors are no longer choosing between performance and sustainability; they’re demanding both, and at the highest levels, they’re willing to pay for it.

Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna has previously stated that the company sees electric vehicles as ‘an opportunity, not a threat.’ The Luce’s auction result seems to validate that stance, proving that the brand’s mystique can transcend powertrain. For a company that has built its identity on the roar of a V12, the silence of an electric Ferrari may yet roar the loudest in the marketplace. As one collector put it after the sale, ‘It’s not just a car. It’s the future—wrapped in a legend.’
